episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Thursday, March 19, 2026. Here's what's happening in A.I. and higher education.
-
Today, a new fellowship program aims to develop A.I. governance professionals across Africa, recognizing that frameworks developed elsewhere may not directly translate.
-
In Insights and Trends today, Lawyers Hub has launched the Africa A.I. Policy Fellowship, a three-month program designed to develop emerging and mid-career professionals in artificial intelligence governance and regulatory frameworks.

According to Global South Opportunities, the fellowship combines academic training, mentorship, and hands-on policy engagement. It targets policy analysts, legal professionals, researchers, academics, technology specialists, and development practitioners.

The program explicitly focuses on developing policy recommendations tailored to African contexts, recognizing that A.I. governance frameworks developed in other regions may not directly translate. The fellowship emphasizes bridging the gap between academic learning and real-world policy engagement.

The application process is designed to be accessible at seven minutes. The three-month intensive format targets working professionals who need focused, practical training rather than comprehensive degree programs. The fellowship emphasizes building networks of professionals capable of influencing national and regional policy discussions.
-
Also in Insights and Trends, an NPR report finds college faculty and students are creating divergent A.I. policies in their classrooms.

According to NPR, Professor Dan Cryer at Johnson County Community College opposes A.I. in writing, comparing it to, quote, bringing a forklift to the gym, end quote. In contrast, Professor Leslie Clement at Johnson C. Smith University embraces A.I. as a, quote, powerful collaborator, end quote, and co-created a course on African Diaspora and A.I.
-
In another Insights and Trends story, College Board research surveying more than 3,000 faculty finds 74 percent report students using A.I. to write essays.

According to the College Board, 84 percent of faculty agree A.I. reduces critical thinking and originality among students. Faculty at selective institutions and writing-intensive disciplines express significantly greater concerns than STEM and business faculty.
-
Turning to Practical Tips, the UCI Digital Learning Lab and School of Education will launch an Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education course for instructors starting summer 2026.

According to New University, the online course will be delivered synchronously over Zoom. It is tailored for faculty, lecturers, and supporting staff seeking to integrate A.I. into their teaching. UC Irvine positions this as professional development for educators navigating the A.I. transition.
-
That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.
